title: Landscape Analysis of the Application of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Regulatory Submissions for Drug Development From 2016 to 2021

content.abstract_summary: A 4-page FDA-internal landscape analysis by 13 CDER/CDRH scientists characterizing the volume, types, and trajectory of AI/ML use in regulatory submissions (IND, NDA, ANDA, BLA, CPIM, DDT) from 2016 to 2021. Total submissions containing AI/ML keywords: 158 (1, 1, 3, 7, 14, 132 by year), with a dramatic ~10-fold jump from 2020 to 2021. The vast majority (140/158) occurred at the clinical development stage; oncology dominated by therapeutic area. Six analysis types and nine application objectives are catalogued (Figure 2). Authors conclude the regulatory use of AI/ML will continue to increase, and signal ongoing FDA capacity-building to evaluate these submissions. The 2022 paper is the empirical baseline that directly motivated the 2025 FDA AI draft guidance (fda_ai_guidance_2025).
key_findings: AI/ML-containing CDER submissions grew from 1/year in 2016–2017 to 132 in 2021 alone — an approximately 10-fold jump from 2020 (14) to 2021 (132); 2017–2020 growth was 2–3× annually
Total 158 submissions 2016–2021 identified by searching CDER databases for 'machine learning' or 'artificial intelligence' across IND, NDA, ANDA, BLA, CPIM, and Drug Development Tools submissions
Most submissions occurred at the clinical development stage (140/158); drug discovery/repurposing (4), nonclinical (8), and postmarketing (6) each accounted for fewer than 10 submissions
Oncology was the leading therapeutic area; psychiatry, gastroenterology, and neurology followed — consistent with data-rich disease areas and biomarker-heavy trial designs

Six AI/ML analysis types identified in submissions: outcome prediction, covariate selection/confounding adjustment, pharmacometric modeling, anomaly detection, imaging/video/voice analysis, RWD phenotyping/NLP

Nine application objectives identified: drug discovery/repurposing, drug toxicity prediction, enrichment design, patient risk stratification/management, dose selection/optimization, adherence monitoring, synthetic control, endpoint/biomarker assessment, postmarketing surveillance

FDA frequency counts likely underestimate actual AI/ML use: 'the frequency by which AI/ML is mentioned in regulatory submissions to the FDA likely only represents a fraction of its increasingly widespread use in drug discovery'
FDA and other regulators jointly identified 10 Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP) guiding principles in 2021 (originally for medical devices, but noted as applicable to drug development)
limitations: Search limited to submissions mentioning 'machine learning' or 'artificial intelligence' by keyword — submissions using AI/ML without these exact terms are missed; authors themselves note this is likely a fraction of actual use
Covers CDER submissions only (drug/biologics); CDRH (device) AI/ML submissions not included in counts, though Diamond MC (CDRH) is a co-author
No statistical modeling of trends — descriptive counts only; no causal analysis of drivers of the 2021 spike
4-page Perspectives piece: examples of each category are illustrative, not exhaustive; analysis type and objective categories are not mutually exclusive
Disclaimer: 'The contents of this article reflect the views of the authors and should not be construed to represent the FDA's views or policies'

gaps_addressed: Provides the empirical baseline — 158 submissions, 2016-2021, 10× jump in 2021 — that justifies the urgency of the WG's regulatory alignment work and the FDA's 2025 guidance

The six analysis types and nine objectives in Figure 2 map directly onto the WG's four pillars: pharmacometric modeling → hybrid_foundations; dose optimization → optimal_control_rl; biomarker assessment/anomaly detection → uq_identifiability; imaging/NLP → generative_ai

The 'fraction of actual use' caveat is an important rhetorical point for WG white papers arguing that the pharmacometrics community must proactively engage with AI/ML even if regulatory submissions don't yet reflect full industry adoption
